hook: Out of every major American company in history, only eleven made the leap from ordinary to extraordinary and held it for fifteen years. None of them did it the way you would expect.

p: Jim Collins had written a bestseller about enduring great companies. Over dinner, a McKinsey consultant told him it was useless, because those companies had been great practically from birth, shaped by founders like Packard and Merck. Most of us, he said, run companies that are pretty good and have no idea how to change that. Collins eventually admitted he was right, and spent five years finding out.

The standard was brutal. Fifteen years of merely average results, then a transition point, then fifteen years of returns at least three times the market, and the leap had to be independent of the industry, so the direct competitors could not have done it too. Eleven companies passed. Walgreens, Kimberly-Clark, Nucor, Wells Fargo, Gillette, Kroger, Abbott and a few others. Unglamorous names. And for each one, Collins paired a direct competitor with the same opportunities in the same era who never made the leap, which turned a study into something close to a controlled experiment.
sections.pull: Good is the enemy of great. We do not have great schools principally because we have good schools.

p: Collins told his team to downplay executives, tired of the story that credits the CEO for everything. The data kept shoving leadership back at him, but not the leadership anyone expected. The transformational leaders were quiet, humble, self-effacing, even shy. He calls them Level 5: extreme personal humility fused with intense professional will, where the ambition is for the institution rather than the self.

Darwin Smith of Kimberly-Clark was an awkward in-house lawyer in unfashionable suits. Two months into the job he was told he had cancer and less than a year to live. He informed the board he had no intention of dying or resigning, drove weekly from Wisconsin to Houston for radiation, and ran the company for twenty more years. He also sold the paper mills, the company's hundred year old core identity, to fight Procter and Gamble in consumer products. The press called it stupid. Kimberly-Clark went on to beat them.

Colman Mockler of Gillette fought off three hostile takeovers, personally telephoning hundreds of elderly shareholders to explain why the coming Sensor razor made the buyout a bad deal. He was right by a factor of three. In January 1991 he was walking down the hall reviewing the proof of a Forbes cover about the company's triumph when he suffered a fatal heart attack, still holding the pages.
sections.pull: In success they look out the window and give away the credit. In failure they look in the mirror.

p: Conventional wisdom says set the vision, then hire people to execute it. The great companies flipped it. They got the right people on the bus and the wrong people off before deciding where to drive. If people join because of the destination, a change of direction loses them. If they join because of who else is aboard, the destination can change freely.

Dick Cooley at Wells Fargo could see banking deregulation coming and had no idea what the industry would look like afterwards. So he simply hired the best people he could find, often with no specific job in mind, on the theory that he would need the strongest crew in banking when the storm hit. He was right. Bank of America, following a weak generals and strong lieutenants model, lurched and lost over a billion dollars in three years.

Collins also went looking hard for a link between executive pay schemes and the leap, and found nothing at all. Compensation is not how you get the right behaviour from the wrong people. It is how you keep the right people on the bus.

Admiral Jim Stockdale was the highest ranking American officer in the Hanoi Hilton, tortured over twenty times across eight years. Collins asked how he survived. I never lost faith that I would prevail, Stockdale said, and would turn it into the defining event of my life. Then Collins asked who did not make it out. Oh, that's easy, said Stockdale. The optimists. They said we'd be out by Christmas, and Christmas came and went. Then Easter. Then Thanksgiving. Then Christmas again. They died of a broken heart.
Never confuse faith that you will prevail in the end, which you can never afford to lose, with the discipline to confront the most brutal facts of your current reality. Hold both, simultaneously.

The corporate version is two grocery chains. In 1953 A and P was one of the largest companies on earth and Kroger was nobody. Both saw the same brutal fact, that shoppers wanted big stores with everything under one roof. Kroger methodically replaced or rebuilt every single store. A and P actually opened an experimental superstore called the Golden Key, watched it work, and closed it, because the answers did not fit what they wanted to believe. Kroger became number one. A and P slid into irrelevance.
sections.pull: The optimists died because they had the faith but not the facts.

p: The fox knows many things, the hedgehog knows one big thing. The fox is cunning, fast, endlessly inventive, and it loses to the hedgehog every time, because the hedgehog just rolls into a ball of spikes. The good-to-great leaders were hedgehogs, simplifying a complex world into a single organising idea. The comparison companies were foxes: scattered, inconsistent, chasing everything.

The concept lives where three circles overlap. What can you be the best in the world at, and just as important, what can you not be best at? What drives your economic engine, expressed as a single ratio of profit per something? And what are you deeply passionate about? Walgreens realised it could be best at convenient drugstores, and that the driver was not profit per store but profit per customer visit, which made expensive corner locations suddenly obvious. Nucor drove profit per ton of finished steel. Wells Fargo, profit per employee.

Abbott shows the discipline of the first circle. In 1964 it admitted it would never be the best pharmaceutical company in the world, because Merck owned that ground. So it found something nobody was fighting over: making health care more cost-effective. These concepts took roughly four years to emerge, usually through a standing group that met to argue and test ideas, which Collins calls a Council. The simplicity sits on the far side of complexity, not the near side.

Most companies add bureaucracy to compensate for the wrong people, and the bureaucracy then drives away the right ones. The great companies broke the cycle by getting disciplined people first, so they never needed the controls. Freedom and responsibility within a framework, and the framework is the hedgehog.

Nucor built its mills in rural Southern farming communities specifically to hire farmers, people who get up at dawn and do what needs doing. Work teams were paid on production with bonuses that could double a wage and vanish entirely for bad steel. No executive dining room, no reserved parking, everyone on the same insurance, and every employee's name printed on the cover of the annual report. Their steelworkers were among the best paid in the industry and their cost per ton was the lowest.

Collins redefines budgeting as the hardest discipline of all. It is not about deciding how much each activity gets. It is about deciding which activities should be fully funded and which should not be funded at all. Selling the paper mills was the most extreme stop-doing decision in the book. Most of us do not have a to-do problem. We have a stop-doing problem.
sections.pull: A world-class triathlete rinsed his cottage cheese to get the last of the fat off. That is the flavour of it.

p: Picture a metal disc thirty feet across weighing many tons. You push. Nothing. You push again and it moves an inch. Hours later it completes one turn. Then two, four, eight, thirty two, a thousand, and at some point its own momentum takes over and it flies. Which push made it go so fast? The question is absurd. It was all of them.

From the outside these transformations looked like sudden revolutionary breakthroughs. From the inside there was no defining moment, no launch event, no slogan. When researchers asked executives what the turning point had been, many were genuinely puzzled by the question and said some version of, it was obvious, we just kept doing what made sense.

The failures ran the opposite pattern, which Collins calls the doom loop. Dramatic new programmes, a savior chief executive with a bold vision, a reorganisation, a big acquisition, then abandonment when instant results did not arrive, then the next lurch. Push the flywheel one way, stop, push it the other. Two great mediocrities never make one great company.

takeaways: Practise the window and the mirror deliberately this week: point out the window when something goes well and into the mirror when it goes badly.
Before you set any new goal, fix the who. Ask of each person, if this were a hiring decision rather than a firing one, would I hire them again.
Move your best people onto your biggest opportunity, not your biggest problem. Managing problems only keeps you good.
Write down the brutal fact you have been avoiding, and hold it next to a written statement of why you will prevail anyway. Both, at the same time.
Work out your own profit per x: the single ratio that, if you increased it steadily, would change your economics most.
Build a stop-doing list as seriously as your to-do list, and fund nothing that falls outside your three circles.
Stop waiting for one decisive push. Pick the direction and commit to turning the same flywheel consistently for the next twelve months.
